text: Cassini had to dive into Saturn to keep the probe away from moons like Enceladus and Titan. Those moons have water, organic chemistry, and other clues that might make life possible, so a spacecraft with Earth microbes on its surfaces could spread them. The probe also had very little propellant left, so a controlled deorbit was the only reliable way to end the mission. On its final orbit, Cassini entered Saturn's atmosphere and was destroyed before it could reach a moon. That protected those worlds from biological contamination, which is the standard planetary protection rule for possible-habitat moons.

The stationary leg hurts because it bears the entire weight of the body and has to stabilize the skateboard while the other leg is pushing. When the pushing leg extends at the hip and knee to generate force, the planted leg takes all the downward and forward forces. This constant bracing puts sustained load on the quadriceps and hamstrings. The muscles in the planted leg get fatigued from holding the position. A lot of skaters report pain in the thigh or calf after long sessions. The lower back takes strain too, since it has to balance the board. Tight hip flexors or a weak core can make this worse. I have noticed this myself when I try to skate further than my fitness level allows. The pain is a sign that the leg muscles are tired from stabilizing the board. Resting the leg for a day or two usually clears it up. Doing some basic leg stretches and building up the pushing leg strength helps prevent it coming back. The push leg also has to flex and extend rapidly, adding to the overall fatigue. The stationary leg acts as a shock absorber for the whole body. For new skaters, the sudden demand on these muscles causes the ache. The push leg needs strong glutes and core to keep the board level. Many people skip this training and end up with soreness. I found that adding some squats and lunges to my routine helped my legs handle the load better. The pain usually fades once the muscles recover from the sustained hold. Adjusting the stance helps. Keeping the knees bent slightly helps absorb the shock. This reduces the direct load on the stationary leg. The board itself also plays a role. A lower deck or stiffer trucks can change how the force is distributed. Swapping out worn-out wheels or adding a different type of grip tape won't fix the muscle fatigue. The core also has to work hard to keep the board from tilting.

The term points to ancestry, not present residence or birthplace. African American, sometimes written as Afro-American, refers to people in the US who trace their lineage to Africa, even if they were born and raised in the country. Most Black Americans did not migrate recently from Africa; many have American generations of family history, often tied to the trans-Atlantic slave trade and to West and Central Africa. The label is an identity term, like Italian-American or Chinese-American, and it marks shared heritage. Some Black people in the US come from the Caribbean, Latin America, South America, or other regions, and the broader phrase can be used loosely to include them. That does not make every Black American a newcomer from Africa. The hyphenated form is less common than African American, but it carries the same idea: the person has African roots, not necessarily an African passport or address. If a Black person was born in the USA but their great-grandparents came from Nigeria, Ghana, or the Caribbean, they can still identify with that heritage. The name tracks descent and culture rather than migration status. The name is about where the bloodline and history begin, not where the person currently lives.

Syrians mainly get weapons through smuggling across the Turkish, Iraqi and Lebanese borders, from captured military warehouses, and from local black markets. In many towns, dealers resell captured rifles, pistols, ammunition and light machine guns, and some fighters are supplied by their own faction or by neighbouring states. The flow still happens because the war has not ended everywhere, local groups need arms to defend neighbourhoods and roads, and smuggling routes remain open. Corruption and armed militias keep buying and storing weapons, so the supply does not stop when major front lines shift. Even in relatively calm districts, people stockpile small arms.

Not all drugs are bad. A drug is a molecule that changes body function, and that includes aspirin, insulin, opioids, and cocaine. The word drug is often used too narrowly. If bad means unsafe at some dose, then even water can be bad in excess. Dose and individual biology decide most of the harm, but the reward system also decides whether a person wants more. The ones people call bad are the psychoactive ones, because they change the brain's reward and stress systems. If a substance produced intense euphoria without adverse effects, it would need to stimulate the same pathways that natural signals use. In the brain, dopamine and serotonin systems can be activated by many molecules, and the stronger the activation, the more likely the system adapts. That adaptation shows up as tolerance and withdrawal; dependence follows. A drug that works strongly on one target still has to interact with the rest of the chemistry around it. The body responds to anything that changes the expected state, whether the change comes from a natural signal or a drug.

There are a few candidates that fit the good-drug idea more closely than opioids or stimulants. Low-dose MDMA is the example people often bring up. It has mood effects without the strong compulsive pattern seen with heroin or cocaine. It still has adverse effects: dehydration and temperature problems, and in some people an unusual sensitivity to social cues. It is often described as having lower abuse liability, not zero. A truly zero-adverse-effect intense-euphoria drug would have to be specific enough to avoid polypharmacology, stable enough that the brain does not downregulate its targets, and it would need to be non-sedating and non-toxic at the doses that produce the desired feeling. That combination is hard because the brain's homeostasis is built to resist persistent deviation. If a molecule keeps pushing the reward system, the system dials itself down. If use stops, the system may overshoot and cause crash-like effects. So even a very selective drug can cause some degree of rebound or withdrawal.

The practical point is that intense pleasure and zero adverse effects are partly at odds. The stronger the euphoria, the stronger the homeostatic correction. That is why classic high-potency drugs have well-documented problems. A perfectly benign strong euphoric is possible in principle, but we do not have one yet. The best examples are still less harmful, not harmless.

I know what you mean, I get it too. It’s not just normal headache territory. The long walk, the noise, the crowds and poor air, plus being distracted by my wife’s opinions all day, leave me with a dull ache behind the eyes and pressure at the temples. The pain is real and it sticks around even after we sit down. It feels different from a regular headache, and I don’t have a medical label for it.

Hi [name],
Your brother was testing your attention. Saying “silk” five times and spelling it keeps the mind on that word. When he follows up with the cow question, the strong cow-milk association can pull out “milk” before the actual question registers. This is a priming or mental-set effect: repeated exposure to one word makes related associations more available.
I’d guess the silk repetition is less important than keeping attention occupied for a few seconds. A casual question then catches you in a loose state, so the automatic association wins. Try it on a coworker or family member; they usually make the same mistake too. The whole exercise is a small attention check for casual, everyday conversation. You can repeat the trick yourself, because the answer feels too familiar to override. The word pair is too familiar, and the automatic association wins very quickly in most people, usually.
cheers,
[You]

Hi Sam,

Thanks for the message. House buying is mostly a sequence of checks and paperwork, and the biggest surprises usually come from skips in that process.

Start with the mortgage. Get an agreement in principle before you look seriously at properties, but remember it is not a guarantee. Then have a building survey and a legal review before you commit. The survey is the document that shows the actual condition of the house, including structural issues. The solicitor checks title, restrictions, and whether the plans match the legal description.

The deposit is usually around 10% of the purchase price, and it is paid when contracts are exchanged. Do not exchange contracts until the survey and legal work are done. Completion is when money is transferred and the keys change hands, usually a few weeks after exchange.

The main things that go wrong are a seller pulling out, a missing survey finding, or a valuation coming in lower than the offer. Ask for the bank's mortgage valuation and an independent building survey separately; the two are not the same. A fixed-rate mortgage removes interest-rate risk for a period, but it does not remove the risk of property problems.

Hey,

A 3-in-1 bodywash/shampoo/conditioner is basically a single formula meant to handle both skin and hair in one wash. The difference from separate bodywash, shampoo, and conditioner is that it has to work on two very different surfaces. Skin and hair respond to different things, so the 3-in-1 has to balance mildness for skin with enough cleaning and conditioning action for hair.

Compared with a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner, the 3-in-1 includes surfactants and additives suited to washing the whole body. A 2-in-1 is aimed only at hair, so its formula can be more aggressive on hair without worrying about skin irritation. That means the 3-in-1 tends to be milder, but it may not clean hair as well as a dedicated shampoo, and it may not condition as well as a dedicated conditioner.

Hi Tom,

They measure continental motion mainly with GPS stations fixed to bedrock and spread across a continent. Each station is anchored to the crust so its coordinates track the motion of that part of the plate. Surveyors take position fixes repeatedly over months and years, then compare them with a global reference frame. The change in position, divided by time, gives a velocity, usually expressed in millimetres per year. Satellite geodesy supports the work. GPS gives the station positions. SLR and VLBI help calibrate the reference frame. A single continent is not perfectly rigid, so velocities differ by location. Plates move only a few centimetres per year, while local tectonic activity can make particular spots move faster. The method treats the Earth's surface as a network of measuring points that record how each part of a plate drifts relative to its neighbours. Modern networks include hundreds of stations. Their combined data let geodesists model plate boundaries. When you look at North America, the Pacific coast moves differently from the Great Lakes region. Repeated fixes over years reduce short-term noise. The resulting velocities show whole-plate drift plus local deformation. It is practical and fairly direct. That is the standard field method used by survey teams.

cheers
Sam

Inbreeding lowers average offspring IQ by raising the chance that harmful recessive variants are inherited from both parents. Related people carry overlapping sets of genes. A child from two unrelated parents usually has a mix of different alleles, while a child from cousins or closer relatives is more likely to get the same rare defect twice. When a harmful recessive allele is present on both chromosomes, it can affect brain development and general cognitive function. Many genes contribute to IQ, so small harmful mutations often interact and compound. This is called inbreeding depression: more inbreeding usually means lower fitness and more recessive disease risk. Related parents also pass on shared family variants. For the wiki, I would state it as: inbreeding increases homozygosity, and that extra pairing of rare bad variants is the main scientific reason offspring cognition can be below the population average. For new colleagues, I find this framing easier to explain.

Hitting an arm often hurts less than hitting the chest or back because the arm has fewer pain-sensitive areas and you can keep it still while other parts are harder to protect. The arm is not among the most sensitive regions. When you are shot or stabbed in the arm, the immediate reaction is usually more manageable, and people can brace the limb or hold it still. The sensation depends on the depth and what tissue is damaged. A deep stab can hurt far more than a shallow graze. The arm gives more control over how the injury is managed, and that control changes how much pain is reported. People often expect an arm injury to be less serious, and that expectation changes how the pain is perceived. There is no rule that says every arm injury is mild. It comes from the arm’s nerve density and from personal expectation.

Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it binds to hemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen. The CO-hemoglobin complex is called carboxyhemoglobin. CO has roughly 200 to 250 times the affinity for hemoglobin that oxygen has. A person breathing a CO-containing gas mixture can carry less oxygen to tissues even if the air still contains oxygen. CO also binds to cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria and interferes with cellular respiration. These effects make CO a potent asphyxiant at low concentrations.

In buildings, CO often comes from gas boilers, furnaces, fireplaces, or small engine exhaust. It is colorless and odorless, so a person cannot smell a leak. A carbon monoxide alarm detects it, but alarms need maintenance and battery checks. That practical note helps a new colleague understand why CO requires monitoring.

Carbon dioxide behaves differently. It is a normal waste product of metabolism and is normally exhaled. At moderate concentrations it is not strongly toxic. At high concentrations, CO2 displaces oxygen in the air and can cause asphyxia; it is used in some fire suppression systems. The difference is that CO chemically blocks oxygen uptake in blood, while CO2 mainly matters when it lowers the oxygen fraction enough to suffocate.

Early symptoms of CO exposure include headache, dizziness and reduced coordination; loss of consciousness follows when oxygen delivery is poor. CO2 at elevated levels causes drowsiness and a tingling sensation, but moderate levels are routinely present indoors. This helps explain why CO can be dangerous in an apparently well-ventilated room, while CO2 is manageable until concentrations become high.

New colleagues should know that CO is dangerous in small doses because it hides in blood, while CO2 requires high levels to become hazardous by lowering available oxygen.

Bracing reduces injury in a crash by limiting how far the body moves and keeping the neck, spine and internal organs from slamming into the plane. During a hard landing or impact, inertia carries us forward and down. The brace position limits that motion. We keep the head low, close to the knees, and hold our hands over or around the knees. Feet stay flat on the floor. The back is kept reasonably straight and the breath is held briefly.

This alignment spreads the load across the legs and pelvis instead of the neck or spine. A forward or downward jolt can bend the neck too far, pinch or fracture the cervical spine, or jam the abdomen. By lowering the head and gripping the knees, the head is cushioned by the legs and the chest and abdomen are less likely to compress the liver, spleen and stomach. Bracing also keeps the hands in place, which reduces the chance of broken arms or fingers striking the armrests. This is the position flight attendants demonstrate and check during briefings. We hold it until told to relax. It reduces the damage an impact can cause, and it does not stop the impact.

Well-known brands mostly appeared after the industrial era began. Pre-industrial businesses were mostly small and local, tied to particular owners or craftsmen. Their names did not travel far, and there were no mass advertising or nationwide supply chains to make those names household names.

Industrial-era changes, including factories, railways, telephones, and printed advertising, created the conditions for businesses to build national recognition. Old firms often merged or changed names, and some went out of business. Companies that survived the shift had to adapt to new markets and new production methods. This explains why the famous brands we know today mostly date from the industrial period.

The bank was cheaper for me because the dealer’s lower rate was the headline, not the total cost. When I shopped for a 2021 Honda CR-V, the local Honda dealer advertised a 1.9% special APR, which looked much better than the 5.25% bank rate I was quoted. I took the car to the dealer’s finance office, and they wrote out a loan at the advertised rate. The paperwork showed the low rate, but also listed a $1,495 documentation fee, a $2,300 extended service plan, and a $750 dealer protection plan. The bank offered a straightforward loan at 5.25%, with only a $95 origination fee. The dealer’s 1.9% rate made the monthly payment look small, but the extra charges made the total amount financed larger. I compared the two offers side by side. The bank loan’s total of principal plus interest came out lower than the dealer package once all fees were included. The dealer’s rate was a hook. The bank’s rate was higher, but the package had fewer add-ons and less friction. I chose the bank loan and paid the $95 fee upfront. The dealer’s advertised rate was lower, but the cost of financing through them included fees that the bank did not. My car was a 1995 Toyota Corolla, and I financed $8,200 at the bank’s 4.9% rate over 48 months. The dealer’s $4,100 loan at 2.9% looked attractive, but the $1,200 dealer fee and $600 maintenance package pushed the total cost above the bank offer. The low rate did not make the dealer financing cheaper. The bank was the better deal in total cost. I have been paying the bank loan since then, and the monthly amount has stayed the same. The dealer’s low rate was the part that made me double-check the paperwork before signing. I found the fee line items and the add-on products, and the bank’s simpler loan was the lower total. That experience is why I think bank financing can be cheaper even when the dealer advertises a lower interest rate.

I find the way US states handle marijuana legality hard to follow, and I’m in favor of making it legal in more of them. I’m glad Colorado has been doing this since 2014. California, Colorado, and New York all allow adults to use and sell it, while Florida only permits it for medical patients. Meanwhile, federal law still keeps cannabis on Schedule I, so someone can legally buy a bud in Denver and have their business’s bank account frozen, or get arrested if they drive across a state line into a state with stricter rules. That mismatch is what bugs me. I’d rather see Congress drop the old schedule and let each state set its own rules, with clear interstate guidelines for people who move. Legalization isn’t complete until the federal and state laws line up, and right now they don’t. The patchwork keeps changing, and I like that direction.

I still remember the first time I read that my neurons fire like tiny sparks. It is not magic. The cell membrane separates charges, and ion channels open or close. When a signal starts moving down an axon, sodium rushes in, making the inside positive for a brief moment. Potassium leaves afterward. The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to restore the gradient. I find that small detail useful: the electricity in the body is made from ion flow. My brain runs on this same electrochemical trick. That is how nerve and muscle cells generate tiny electrical pulses constantly inside each cell.

For me, sampling is a listening habit before it is a technical step. I start by sitting with a turntable or a hard drive full of old records, and I look for a short piece of music that has a groove I want to build around. Usually it is a two or three bar drum break, a bass line, a horn stab, or a vocal phrase. I am not looking for a whole song, which seems backwards to me. I am looking for a fragment that can be looped or stretched into a rhythm section.

The source matters. A scratched 78 rpm record, a warped 45, a tape with hiss, a digital file from a CD all change what I can do. If the original is noisy, I spend time cleaning the audio before I use it. I will lower the pitch a half step, slice a drum hit into one second pieces, or trim the ends so the loop point is clean. A sample that jumps badly at the loop makes the whole track sound broken.

In my own sessions, I often put a short loop into Ableton, chop it, reverse a fragment, and add compression or a filter. I have also used an MPC when I want that hardware feel. A hardware sampler gives me a certain attack and quantization, and that matters when the rest of the track is played live.

I do not think old sources automatically sound better. A 1960s soul record has dust noise and a limited frequency range, while a 1980s rap sample has a cleaner signal. I pick what fits the track. A 1970s disco fragment works when the rhythm is tight and the bass line is warm. A 1990s R&B phrase works when it already has a modern feel.

The rights side of sampling is a separate problem, and I do not want to get into that here. What matters to me is that I can take a short piece of music, break it apart, and make it into something new. The skill is choosing a fragment that carries a feeling, and making it sit under the other parts. If the sample is loud, I turn it down and add low end or percussion. If the sample is short, I stretch it and accept that the pitch will shift. I am trying to use the source as an instrument.

My headache isn't my skull hurting; the skull is dense bone and not very sensitive to pain. The pain comes from the membranes and blood vessels wrapped around the brain. When a vessel gets inflamed or a membrane is irritated, the body sounds the alarm, and that is what I feel as a headache. I treat it as a warning light, not as damage to my head. When my head aches, I keep a short list of the usual suspects, like a stiff neck, a change in air pressure, or a night of poor sleep. I keep that list on a sticky note on my desk. I try to match the pain to the trigger instead of just taking a pill. The pain is the body's way of saying something is off, and knowing what caused it is what I want to figure out every time.

I can't tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, choosing this place specifically because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it'd be easy. We entered our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15! It was just a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night is not completely wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars if it were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and, surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two of us came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I had expected to pay at one.

I was disappointed that steak wasn't offered. At that price, I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was that there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

Overall, I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so example becomes eexample and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once in the afternoon, always while typing fast and not looking.

I paid 38 dollars and kept it because of the switches. I asked the seller what they were, and the answer took a week. By that point I had already pried off a keycap and found out for myself. They were brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I would have been without a keyboard while waiting. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

About two years ago, we called Rockmount Ranch Wear and ordered two shirts for my father. They never arrived. The sales rep wrote our delivery address wrong: she wrote the 7 in 5407 as a 1, so the shirts went to 5401. The people at 5401 took the box to the local UPS store to return it. Then it disappeared and we did not hear from them again. We only found out several weeks later. During the dispute, we placed another order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first pair. The owner took it up. He agreed the shipment went to the wrong address, but he said they would not issue a refund until the shirts came back. He said we shared the blame because we had not been friendly enough with the people at 5401, which is only four doors away. We disputed the original card charge, and eventually our credit-card company gave us a credit.
